title: Polymarket says annualized revenue has topped $1.8 billion
description: A Polymarket advertisement at a metro station in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPrediction mark
body: A Polymarket advertisement at a metro station in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPrediction market platform Polymarket has surpassed $1.8 billion in annualized revenue, the company told CNBC on Tuesday.That's up from June, when Polymarket disclosed that its annual revenue run rate was north of $1 billion, following the launch of its domestic exchange in May. Polymarket's revenue is being fueled by growth in that U.S. exchange, which operates as a separate trading venue from its decentralized finance international platform. The domestic exchange saw more than $14.5 billion in notional volume in October, up from $4 billion in June, according to data analytics platform TickerTracker. That increase has been driven by a series of highly traded events, including the FIFA World Cup over the summer and the start of the NFL season in September. Volume has been supported by the growing popularity of Combo event contracts, which work similarly to sportsbooks' multi-leg parlays, accounted for more than 70% of volume traded on the platform on Sunday. The revenue growth since June also comes after the company began a fresh $1 billion funding round that values Polymarket at $21 billion. Polymarket still faces near-term headwinds, though. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is conducting a broad investigation into the company, with questions surrounding advertising practices and whether the company in the past violated a settlement with the agency to bar U.S. residents from accessing its international exchange. The company also may face increased scrutiny from a Democratic congress, partially due to the position of President Donald Trump's son — Donald Trump Jr. — as an advisor to the company. But Polymarket previously told CNBC it would work with lawmakers as they begin to understand the growing prediction market industry. "We welcome scrutiny," a spokesperson said. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Polymarket says annualized revenue has topped $1.8 billion

title: Does anyone feel safe from layoffs right now?
description: In late October, Bashel Lubarsky had a feeling something was off when she got a DM from her co-worker on the way to work. Once she opened her email an
body: In late October, Bashel Lubarsky had a feeling something was off when she got a DM from her co-worker on the way to work. Once she opened her email and saw a note announcing layoffs, Lubarsky suspected she'd been cut.Minutes later, Lubarsky stepped off the subway to join an impromptu Zoom meeting with HR and got laid off in the middle of downtown Brooklyn, New York.Up until that point, Lubarsky, 28, says she held two ideas in her head: On the one hand, she had a feeling the company would be going through another round of October layoffs considering it had done the same in 2025. On the other, she felt pretty secure in her job as a graphic designer and illustrator. She'd gotten a promotion earlier in the year, had essential skills used across multiple projects and jokes that she was likely the "cheapest" member of her team. "I never thought my job wasn't safe," Lubarsky tells CNBC Make It.Lubarsky's experience hits home for many Americans these days. Despite official numbers saying the job market is relatively stable, with new jobs opening up, increased hiring and a steady unemployment rate, an increasing number of workers can't shake the feeling that layoffs are just around the corner and that nothing — not an artificial intelligence-related job, stellar performance or company success — is enough to keep them safe.Anxiety is rising despite fewer layoffsAccording to the American Psychological Association's spring survey of 2,009 employed adults, some 32%, or 1 in 3, U.S. workers say they're concerned about losing their job in the next few weeks or months, up from 26% in 2025.U.S. employee engagement fell to 29% in the third quarter of 2026, its lowest level since 2011, according to Gallup. And employee confidence fell to its lowest point in September since Glassdoor began measuring it in 2016; confidence rebounded slightly in October, per Glassdoor's latest analysis, but remains near record lows.Bashel Lubarsky, a graphic designer and illustrator, was laid off from her job in October after being promoted earlier this year.Courtesy of subjectDespite the sour outlook, layoffs are less severe today than they were a year ago. Through October, employers announced 617,189 job cuts, down 44% from the number of layoff notices in the first 10 months of 2025, according to data from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas.The biggest cuts this year are happening in tech, transportation and food, per the report, with companies citing AI as a leading reason for layoffs.It doesn't really matter whether your job can be done by AI or can't be done by AI. It only matters whether the projects that you're working on are part of the company's strategy moving forward in an AI world.Daniel ZhaoGlassdoor chief economistIt's not that companies are outright replacing employees with AI, but rather they're "shifting investment and headcount from one part of the business to another" focused on AI, says Daniel Zhao, chief economist at Glassdoor."Unfortunately for many workers, that resource reallocation story is a scarier one because it doesn't really matter whether your job can be done by AI or can't be done by AI," Zhao says. "It only matters whether the projects that you're working on are part of the company's strategy moving forward in an AI world."Working on AI-related efforts still may not provide security if a company shifts priorities in how it wants to use the new tech. Briana Taylor says she felt secure in her product marketing manager job at Microsoft since it was related to the company's AI products. She says she received "exceeded expectations" remarks on her performance review, scoring her a bonus and level promotion, months before being laid off in June 2025."I feel like right now companies need something to blame, so they're using AI as a scapegoat," says Taylor, 35, of Chicago. "All the layoffs seem to be happening out of left field."The surprise exit influenced her next career moves. Taylor says she took a pay cut in her next job, and she also launched her own AI consultancy for small businesses, dubbed Rethink to Rise AI, as a safety net. Briana Taylor was laid off from her job at Microsoft in 2025. She thought her job was secure because she worked on the company's AI products.Courtesy of subjectStrong performance doesn't guarantee job securityMuch of today's stock market growth is being propped up by expectations of what AI can do as an industry and how that will shape the rest of the economy,  says Jo-Ellen Pozner, associate professor of management at Santa Clara University's Leavey School of Business. That's putting pressure on tech companies in particular: "You've got to put up results," she says. "And in the absence of a blockbuster new product introduction, lowering costs is probably the only way to do that." The introduction of AI and new forms of automation "make it that much more tempting for companies to just get rid of extra headcount," Pozner says.That sometimes means companies are reducing headcount even if they're showing other signs of doing well. Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees in October days before reporting 19% revenue growth year over year in the quarter ending Sept. 30. American Express and Barclays announced 5% cuts to their respective workforces even as the financial services sector sees profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit.Looming layoffs create an "intensely destabilizing" work environment, where employees lacking psychological safety divert their energy from creative and innovative work into their anxiety, Pozner says. "It's very counterproductive, and I think quite short-sighted."In some cases, layoff signals could lead workers to go into overdrive to keep themselves safe. When layoffs are a moving target, it's not always a guarantee. Weeks ago, Sam Epperson, 33, in Colorado Springs, Colo., was told his tech sales team was behind their goals for the year and took it as guidance to pick up the pace. By early October, Epperson says he was able to close a number of deals amounting to $300,000 to bridge the gap.It wasn't enough, and he was laid off before the end of the month. "I very much so felt safe in my position until I was let go," he says.Sam Epperson was laid off from his tech sales job in October after working to close the gap in his team's annual goals.Courtesy of subjectA lackluster job market is keeping workers on edgeWhile economists say there are signs of a slowly improving job market, such as jobs being added to the economy and people feeling confident enough to quit their jobs, "we really are going to need to see consistent improvement in the job market to really make workers feel like things are looking up again," says Zhao of Glassdoor.For her part, Lubarsky in New York City is scaling her own graphic design and illustration client book while looking for a new job. Her outlook isn't great.Lubarsky says she's been applying to jobs for over a year, even while employed. "I am hardworking. I have so many recommendations, referrals [and] clients. I have everything you could need. I can't even get a response saying, 'No, thank you,'" she says.It feels worse than the Covid-19-era job market she entered after college, she says: "I graduated in 2020 into the pandemic, and I still got a job within a year."

title: PepsiCo to cut about 1,000 jobs as North American business struggles
description: Bottles of Pepsi are displayed in a store in New York City on March 17, 2025.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesPepsiCo is cutting about 1,000 jobs across No
body: Bottles of Pepsi are displayed in a store in New York City on March 17, 2025.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesPepsiCo is cutting about 1,000 jobs across North America as the company tries to turn around lagging sales in its home market."We have a clear ambition for PepsiCo North America: to build a stronger, more future-fit business that delivers industry-leading growth," Ram Krishnan, CEO of PepsiCo North America, wrote in a Monday letter to employees obtained by CNBC. "To do that, we need to be faster, more connected, and more capable, while continuing to invest in growth — behind our people, capabilities and brands."Over the next week, Pepsi plans to cut jobs as it says it aims to streamline its operations and better connect teams across the company's North American business. PepsiCo employs about 306,000 people worldwide, including roughly 125,000 in the United States, as of Dec. 27, according to a company filing. The Wall Street Journal first reported the coming layoffs.In October, PepsiCo cut its full-year earnings outlook, citing the struggles in its home market. During the third quarter, its North American beverage unit saw volume shrink 2%, while its North American food division reported flat volume. While the company has tried to boost sales by cutting prices and investing in marketing, the turnaround is taking longer than expected, Chief Financial Officer Steve Schmitt said on the company's earnings conference call.Shares of Pepsi rose slightly in afternoon trading. The stock is down nearly 1% this year, lagging behind the S&P 500's gains of nearly 11% over the same period.

title: 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong
description: FG Construction displays a We're Hiring! sign during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on April 30, 2026 in Su
body: FG Construction displays a We're Hiring! sign during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on April 30, 2026 in Sunrise, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesA little-noticed category in Friday's blockbuster jobs report is challenging the consensus view about job losses caused by artificial intelligence.At least for now, the data suggests the U.S. is gaining jobs as a result of the AI boom, not losing them.And another category suggests the strong jobs numbers could have some staying power.Nonfarm payrolls grew by 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Friday report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It was a surprising surge in hiring that blew way past Wall Street's expectations. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of just 59,000 for the month.Here are three surprising things you might have missed from the report.ConsultingHiring for consultants surged in the month, sending the profession's total head count to a fresh record.The labor force for management, scientific and technical consultants expanded by 17,300 jobs between September and October, the largest month-over-month increase in nearly two years. This category is a subset of the professional and business services sector tracked by BLS and accounted for 25% of the entire sector's gains for the month.What's more, this workforce has grown by more than 45,000 jobs over the past year. That gain pushed the total employee base for these types of workers past 1.9 million for the first time on record, according to BLS data.Hiring in the industry had largely stalled since 2023 following years of rapid expansion during the pandemic. Wall Street has questioned if the rise of artificial intelligence will curb demand for these services. Those fears have led shares of consulting firm Gartner to lose more than half of their value over the past three years. Accenture and FTI Consulting have dropped about 18% and 9% over that period, even as the S&P 500 has climbed roughly 74%. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconGartner vs the S&P 500 over the last 5 yearsNow, some economists are speculating that the recent jump could be driven by businesses hiring consultants to help them adopt AI. Gartner forecast in September that worldwide AI spending would total $2.7 trillion in 2026, a nearly 50% increase year over year."The AI buildout and corporate interests to increase utilization will keep the technical consultants employed," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial.Roach called the consulting sector a bright spot in October that is "worth watching." He noted that these jobs also saw double-digit growth in the late 1990s, as firms raced to implement new internet technology into their businesses.So far, data suggests that AI may be adding more jobs to the labor market than it is taking away through automation. An assessment by Moody's Analytics found that AI has created a net 786,000 jobs since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, driven in part by data center construction."Wasn't AI supposed to destroy jobs? The most dystopian scenarios even called for mass unemployment," Mark Zandi, Moody's chief economist, wrote in a social media post on Monday. "That risk hasn't gone away, and AI-driven productivity gains could still shift into a higher gear. But for now, AI is adding to job growth, not subtracting from it."Temporary hiresHiring of temporary workers also drove growth, which could signal that the labor market is heating up.The subsector's payrolls grew by 18,600 in October, one of its largest month-over-month increases since 2022. This category is another part of the professional and business services sector and accounted for 27% of the sector's gains for the month.The total size of this workforce is still well below record highs set in 2022. But headcount has grown roughly 3% since December and now sits at levels last seen in April 2025, the month that President Donald Trump's rollout of his plan for steep tariffs put corporate America on alert.Economists see temporary hiring as a leading indicator in the labor market. Conventional wisdom suggests that companies that hire new workers on a short-term basis often transition them to full-time roles later.That could be what's happening here, but the fact that the end of the year is approaching makes it harder to tell. The boost could be a result of hiring as the holiday shopping season approaches — and if employers are staffing up for the holidays, they are less likely to retain those workers when January rolls around. Such hiring hasn't typically happened this early, but the season creeps earlier each year. The BLS adjusts its numbers to account for seasonal trends, but won't immediately make an adjustment if the trend is changing. One hint that holiday hiring may be shifting comes in a separate category of workers: couriers and messengers. This is another area that acts as a barometer for holiday labor demand, and just over one out of every 10 new jobs in the month was in this category.That category "bears watching for reversal in the months ahead," said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, a wealth manager.Election spendingHiring related to political campaigns in the final weeks of an expensive election cycle could have also boosted payrolls.Employment in political organizations has historically spiked heading into midterm or presidential elections, according to a BLS analysis. Staffing levels tend to peak in October of those years, the data shows. Nonfarm payrolls expanded in the months before the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections.But the vast size of campaign coffers this cycle may have translated into more jobs than before. The 2026 congressional election is slated to go down in history as the most expensive midterm on record, according to an analysis from OpenSecrets, a money-in-politics watchdog group. Billions of dollars spent on campaigns may have translated into paid gigs that involve door knocking, phone banking or other election-related work.

schema.headline: 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong

title: Children’s Place files for bankruptcy protection, seeks buyer
description: The Children's PlaceJames Leynse | Corbis | Getty ImagesChildren's clothing retailer The Children's Place has filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy protecti
body: The Children's PlaceJames Leynse | Corbis | Getty ImagesChildren's clothing retailer The Children's Place has filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, it said Sunday.The company is looking to sell substantially all of its assets and is seeking offers from potential buyers by Dec. 9, with a goal to close a deal by the end of December. The retailer, whose brands include The Children's Place and Gymboree, says it operates two digital storefronts and 514 North American stores, and has distribution in 13 countries through franchise and wholesale partners. The company's performance has taken a hit in recent years from tariff hikes and slower consumer spending, among other factors.Its stores and e-commerce sites remain open for now, and the company is planning to continue its ongoing inventory sales with court approval. "For nearly 60 years, The Children's Place has supported growing families with apparel that customers have come to know and love. We recognize the significance of this development for our employees, customers, vendors, and other partners, and we are committed to conducting an efficient and transparent sale process," said Rudy Morando, co-chief restructuring officer of The Children's Place. "In the meantime, we remain focused on serving the families who have trusted The Children's Place for generations."This move comes days after interim Children's Place CEO Muhammad Asif Seemab and Chief Strategy Officer Muhammad Umair stepped down from their roles. Seemab and Umair will both remain on the company's board. CFO John Szczepanski took on the role of acting president and principal executive officer.Seemab is also managing director of Saudi-based Mithaq Capital, which took a majority stake in The Children's Place in 2024 when the company was facing financial trouble. Even with support from the investors, the company has not been able to significantly improve its financial outlook. In its bankruptcy filing, the company reported about $742 million in assets, compared to about $881 million in debts. In the second fiscal quarter of 2026, its most recently reported quarter, the company's net sales dropped nearly 19% from the same period the year prior. At the time, Seemab said in a news release that during the quarter the company was "stabilizing our customer file" and "driving traffic to our stores and websites," and saw "lower conversion, combined with a very clearance-heavy mix." He also pointed to tough comparisons to the prior-year period, due in part to back-to-school shopping demand that "was uniquely elevated ... ahead of anticipated tariff price increases."The Children's Place stock has plummeted in recent years and was trading around 18 cents per share on Monday.

title: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than expected, complicating Fed's inflation fight
description: An employee restocks eggs at an H-E-B grocery store on May 11, 2026 in Austin, Texas.Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesCosts for goods and services rose more
body: An employee restocks eggs at an H-E-B grocery store on May 11, 2026 in Austin, Texas.Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesCosts for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation.The consumer price index, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase.Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain.The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%.The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data.Stock market futures drifted lower following the release while Treasury yields jumped. Traders fully priced in a quarter percentage point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9 and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the release, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next move regarding interest rates. At its October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data."This was the report the market could least afford to see," said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. "A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer."Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%.Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%. Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase.Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%.Markets already had been expecting the Fed to hike its benchmark borrowing rate next month, but the inflation data may have sealed the deal.Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December. Waller added that it's important the Fed follow through on expectations for a hike.Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, also speaking Tuesday, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases. Logan noted that the CPI report was "higher than expected" and said she is worried that the Fed's primary inflation-forecasting metric, the personal consumption expenditures price index, also could move higher when it is reported later in November."It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall," she said. "After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate."Despite the moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for some 5½ years.In addition to tariffs and the war, inflation has been pressured by hyperscaler spending in the artificial intelligence buildout. Electricity prices rose 0.9%, a potential complication from the AI story.Consumers, though, continue to spend — retail sales rose 0.8% in September, according to the Commerce Department — and businesses are still raising prices.A net 37% of businesses responding to the October National Federation of Independent Business survey reported that they plan to raise prices in the next three months, the highest level since July 2022.

schema.headline: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than expected, complicating Fed's inflation fight

title: Trump’s C-SPAN call marks latest surprise post-midterm appearance
description: Dana White, president of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), left, and US President Donald Trump during a news conference in the James S. Brady Pres
body: Dana White, president of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), left, and US President Donald Trump during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Trump said the FBI is looking into Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's affair with a woman who is reportedly suspected to have been a Chinese intelligence officer. Photographer: Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump made an unexpected call into C-SPAN's evening broadcast Monday, extending a series of surprise appearances after Republicans' midterm election defeat."It looks like we've got a call from the White House," host Mimi Geerges told viewers as Trump joined the debut of "Washington Journal Primetime."Trump congratulated Geerges on the launch before taking questions on immigration, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Iran war.Asked what he watches on C-SPAN, Trump said he follows viewer call-ins to gauge public sentiment."I like to watch the call-ins because it gives me a little of an indication of where we are," he said.The unannounced, eight-minute call followed another unexpected appearance earlier Monday, when Trump entered the White House briefing room alongside UFC CEO Dana White. Reporters were summoned so quickly that aides did not have time to attach the presidential seal to the podium, according to Reuters.It was Trump's first briefing room appearance in 198 days, according to a White House pool report. With the press secretary post vacant, Trump joked about offering White the job, to which the UFC chief declined.Trump said he had been having "a very bad press day," as he floated White as his next press secretary.Last Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered substantial midterm losses, Trump also abruptly invited reporters to the construction site of his White House ballroom for his first public event since the election.Trump spent more than 20 minutes discussing White House construction and renovation projects, including the ballroom's Corinthian columns, marble flooring and the helipad, before turning to the election results during questions from reporters.US President Donald Trump looks at a steel beam he signed as he speaks at the construction site of the East Wing ballroom at the White House in Washington, DC, on November 4, 2026. Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesWhen asked whether he regretted how his campaign had ended, Trump distanced himself from the Republican losses."If I were on the ballot, we would have won," he said.Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 elections, dealing Trump a major political setback and setting up a divided government when the new Congress takes office in January.Trump has long favored direct telephone contact with the media, including live calls to Fox News programs such as "Fox & Friends" during his first term.CBS News previously reported that Trump personally arranged one such television appearance, while The Associated Press has documented his habit of contacting journalists directly by cellphone to pitch stories and react to live coverage.— CNBC's Daniel Mangan contributed to this story.

schema.headline: Trump’s C-SPAN call marks latest surprise post-midterm appearance

title: Jim Cramer says Anthropic's IPO could make or break the AI trade. Here's why
description: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Mon, Nov 9 20266:30 PM ESTKey PointsJim Cramer said Anthropic's upcoming IPO could be crucial to
body: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Mon, Nov 9 20266:30 PM ESTKey PointsJim Cramer said Anthropic's upcoming IPO could be crucial to a recovery in AI stocks.A disappointing offering could have ripple effects across the industry.watch nowAnthropic's upcoming initial public offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Monday."Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," the "Mad Money" host said, exactly two weeks after the Claude developer filed its S-1 IPO paperwork. Despite the recent sell-off in AI stocks, Anthropic is reportedly moving ahead with its IPO plans. The company is expected to meet with major investors this week and is targeting a trading debut as early as Thursday or Friday of next week, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "I don't think it's hyperbolic to say that this could be one of the most consequential IPOs in history."Cramer explained that the billions of dollars being spent on AI chips and data centers ultimately depend on a handful of AI developers, including Anthropic, generating enough revenue to justify those investments."Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending," Cramer said. "If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today." Cramer pointed to SpaceX as an example of how interconnected the AI trade has become. Much of the Elon Musk rocket and AI company's recent revenue growth has come from renting computing capacity to customers, including Alphabet's Google and Anthropic. Google pays roughly $900 million a month for that capacity, while Anthropic's commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion monthly to more than $3 billion, according to its IPO prospectus.Those contracts allow for SpaceX's massive purchases of Nvidia chips. "But if an Anthropic deal fails?" Cramer said. "Then Anthropic wouldn't have the cash to fulfill its contracts, and you'd have to take down estimates for both SpaceX and Nvidia, along with a whole host of other compute providers to Anthropic, and their suppliers." Not to mention, Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia have all invested in Anthropic, making their earnings sensitive to changes in the AI developer's valuation.The wrinkle here is that investor appetite for an Anthropic IPO appears to be weakening. Anthropic's potential valuation has reportedly fallen from as much as $2 trillion earlier this fall to as low as $1 trillion following last week's technology sell-off on concerns that the Democratic wave in the midterm election will mean slower new data center construction.On Friday, during the CNBC Investing Club's Annual Meeting, Cramer also stressed the importance of the Anthropic offering to the AI trade and to Club portfolio names Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia.watch now

title: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
description: Amazon's Ring unveiled a flying indoor security camera that lets users autonomously check on their home.RingAmazon's Ring is going deeper into surveil
body: Amazon's Ring unveiled a flying indoor security camera that lets users autonomously check on their home.RingAmazon's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.   The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a pre-set path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said. At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights. "If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house."The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne.Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google. Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns, primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called "Search Party." It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety, which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers.  Ring repurposed Amazon's Astro consumer robot, first unveiled in 2021, to be a business security device.RingRing first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam, in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing. The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot, which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces. Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot." Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.  Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device. "People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said. Ring said privacy is the "default" mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they're recording. Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot. "We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside." The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said. schema.headline: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses

title: Lucid misses Wall Street’s earnings expectations, expands loan from Saudi Arabia fund
description: The Lucid Motors Lucid Air electric car at the 91st edition of the International Paris Motor Show at the Porte de Versailles in Paris, Oct. 12, 2026.L
body: The Lucid Motors Lucid Air electric car at the 91st edition of the International Paris Motor Show at the Porte de Versailles in Paris, Oct. 12, 2026.Ludovic Marin | AFP | Getty ImagesLucid Group missed Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as the embattled electric vehicle maker continues an "operational reset" aimed at cutting costs and narrowing losses.The company on Monday also announced a $1.75 billion increase in a delayed draw term loan from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the company's largest shareholder.Lucid stock fell roughly 5% in aftermarket trading Monday.Here's how Lucid performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: $2.74 vs. a loss of $2.28 expectedRevenue: $350 million vs. $407 million expectedDespite the top- and bottom-line misses, the company's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of a loss of $726 million beat Wall Street's expectations of a loss of $611 million for the third quarter. Its net loss for the quarter was $830.9 million, down from a loss of $978.4 million a year earlier.Lucid's 2025 third quarter included revenue of $336.6 million, a loss of $3.31 per share and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $717.7 million.The quarterly results are the first since Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli, who started leading the company in June, announced a restructuring plan that included implementing several cost-cutting efforts and delaying the company's upcoming midsize vehicle from the end of this year until the second half of next."Our transformation is beginning to show progress. We are acting with urgency, strengthening the fundamentals and driving greater discipline, while continuing to invest in the priorities to deliver profitable long-term growth," Napoli said in a release.The company's turnaround plan includes $1.4 billion in cash flow improvements this year as well as focusing attention on a robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro, a factory that's under construction in Saudi Arabia and the midsize vehicle.Lucid said the capital from PIF is expected to give the company "additional financial flexibility as Lucid delivers on its turnaround program." It is expected to assist in funding "operations and key investments" into the fourth quarter of 2027, including the start of production for the midsize vehicle.The additional funds boost Lucid's total liquidity to $3.75 billion, up from $2 billion to end the third quarter."We are grateful for the continued financial support from our anchor shareholder, which further energizes us to remain focused on execution and on our commitments as we build a stronger, sustainable Lucid," Napoli said.Lucid said Monday that the company expects to communicate its midterm plan and targets early next year. The EV maker in May suspended its guidance and many targets, citing new leadership and time needed to develop a turnaround plan.

schema.headline: Lucid misses Wall Street’s earnings expectations, expands loan from Saudi Arabia fund

title: Skydance outlines its $6 billion in planned cost savings. Here's the breakdown
description: David Ellison, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., left, and Ynon Kreiz, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., right, at the New Yor
body: David Ellison, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., left, and Ynon Kreiz, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., right, at the New York Stock Exchange, Oct. 8, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSkydance is pulling back the curtain on how it plans to achieve at least $6 billion in cost savings in the next three years."By combining two global streaming services, two film and TV studio groups, two television portfolios, and overlapping corporate functions, we can reduce duplicative spend across an expense base of more than $50 billion," the company wrote in a letter to shareholders Monday as part of Paramount Skydance's third-quarter earnings release.Skydance, the company formed by the combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, said it projects at least $2.2 billion in cost reductions from eliminating "redundant back-office and corporate functions," including eliminating management layers and ramping the use of artificial intelligence. Those savings also account for "rationalizing" its office footprint. Skydance expects at least $1 billion in savings from streamlining marketing and promotional spending. And around $1.4 billion in savings will come from unifying its streaming businesses and broadcast architecture and integrating back-end technology. A final $1.4 billion in savings will be tied to "optimizing third-party spend," eliminating overlapping expenses, and consolidating purchasing decisions to one centralized group, Skydance said."We are confident in achieving these savings, drawing on our playbook from Paramount," the company wrote. "That program is on track to achieve over $2.7 billion in run-rate efficiencies by the end of 2026."Some of that cost-cutting has already begun. Last month, Skydance began offering voluntary buyouts to employees ahead of official layoffs. At the same time, the company adopted a five-day-per-week in-office policy. Additionally, last week saw the departure of eight executives — four from Warner Bros. and four from Paramount.The company has previously said it plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform. On Monday, Skydance said it would take the first step toward that goal early next year, offering a bundle of the streaming services "at an even greater value."Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told investors during the company's earnings call that Skydance is also looking for ways to optimize its content budget. The company spends more than $30 billion annually on shows and films. "As one company, we can make smarter choices about how we distribute and monetize both new content and library content," Kreiz said.Skydance noted that it's expecting a $200 million headwind in the fourth quarter from theatrical underperformances at Warner Bros. studio related to already launched titles and upcoming releases.The company will also utilize AI to speed up production and decrease costs to make films, co-CEO and chairman David Ellison said on the call."We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budget more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk," Ellison said.The updates came alongside third-quarter results for the legacy Paramount Skydance company that included revenue of $7.03 billion, which was roughly in line with StreetAccount estimates of $7.04 billion, and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $1 billion, topping StreetAccount estimates of $913.5 million. However, adjusted earnings per share of 45 cents were not immediately comparable to StreetAccount EPS estimates. The results don't include the impact of the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, which closed after the end of the third quarter. Skydance detailed business units of the combined entity, including studios, direct-to-consumer and TV, and said it will provide full-year guidance during its fourth-quarter earnings report early next year. "Going forward, we will provide guidance on an annual basis, as we prioritize long-term value creation, which we believe will be more consistent with our strategic approach," the company told shareholders. "We will continue to provide quarterly updates, including certain forward-looking commentary where applicable, which will give investors visibility into our near-term progress of the business."

schema.headline: Skydance outlines its $6 billion in planned cost savings. Here's the breakdown

title: CoreWeave earnings put debt-fueled AI build-out under scrutiny
description: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesCoreWeave faces a pivotal test when it reports its third-quarter financial results after the bell on Tuesday. Th
body: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesCoreWeave faces a pivotal test when it reports its third-quarter financial results after the bell on Tuesday. The market will be closely watching what the neocloud company says about artificial intelligence spending — and how it plans to finance its infrastructure buildout. The outcome could either calm concerns over its debt or stoke more fear. "Investors need neoclouds to quantify how much financing they expect to raise to execute on existing backlog," Wolfe Research said in a note Monday. "We think outlooks that communicate when and which avenues of funding will be tapped will increase investor confidence."CoreWeave stock and bonds have come under pressure as fears deepened about the enormous amount of debt it has taken out to build its data centers.  Its stock is down roughly 40% over the past month. Meanwhile, the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 15.5% on Tuesday, after jumping to 16.7% on Thursday as investors digested the election results and possible roadblocks to data center construction. Bond yields move inversely to prices.CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031The spread on its five-year credit default swaps — which is insurance against default and considered a barometer of perceived credit risk — is also at levels that are considered distressed. On Tuesday, its CDS spread stood around 1,152 basis points, after rising above its October peak to close at 1,278 basis points on Thursday. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.  CoreWeave's five-year credit default swapsIn addition, the New Jersey-based company's leverage is high. CoreWeave has a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from almost 291% a year ago.  CEO Michael Intrator has sought to quell investor fear, posting on LinkedIn after the election last week that the company doesn't anticipate "any impact to CoreWeave's existing customer commitments or associated backlog as a result of shifts in the political landscape." The company reported a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion in the second quarter. It has about $35 billion in debt, as of June 30.Capex watchCoreWeave has already given a picture of what it expects for the third quarter. It guided for quarterly revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion when it reported second-quarter results in August. It anticipated capital expenditures between $11.5 billion and $13.5 billion for the quarter and $35 billion to $39 billion for the full year. The company also expects 1.85 gigawatts in active power by year-end. Wells Fargo expects the company's capex needs for the rest of the year to be largely covered by its remaining undrawn debt, debt issuances in August/September and the $12 billion it is holding for project costs, which will flow into capex, analyst Michael Turrin said in a note Sunday. However, its 2027 capex could reach $66 billion, based on an expected capacity addition of 1.5 gigawatts, Turrin said. That will require at least $25 billion more in debt, he noted. It can be largely funded through delayed draw term loans, which allows CoreWeave to draw down funds over time, and the rest can come through bonds and convertibles, he said. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave year to dateTurrin has an overweight rating and $115 price target on the stock, implying 135% upside from Monday's close. "While neoclouds sit in the eye of the AI storm, we remain confident that CRWV is the highest quality co in the space," Turrin wrote. "Beyond the noise, we see capacity/revs coming in better than expected (1.95GW this yr vs guide 1.85GW) as margins start to inflect."However, investors likely won't get all the answers they're seeking during CoreWeave's third-quarter results, said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin."One of the major issues for CoreWeave is whether or not they can obtain all the financing they need," he said. "They may try and calm the markets, but I'm not sure how much color they can and will provide."Investors will be looking for 2027 guidance on capex and free cash flow, though that may not come until Coreweave releases fourth quarter results, Chalfin notes. CoreWeave could ease investor concerns by showing it has plans and approvals in place to scale capacity through 2027, he said. The company can also demonstrate remaining performance obligation (RPO) growth, which shows the total value of its contracted future revenue, and highlight new customer wins.In addition, pricing has been really strong on recent deals, Chalfin pointed out. "That could show up in an operating margin beat for Q3 and expectations for Q4."Alternate fundingWhile CoreWeave faces finances challenges, the company has many ways to access capital, Chalfin said. That includes chip-backed deals, which allow Corewave to borrow money using GPUs as collateral, and original equipment manufacturer financing. For instance, CoreWeave could turn to Dell, which is a big supplier with a strong balance sheet, Chalfin noted. "Despite all the market sentiment, fundamentals are actually quite strong and pricing is strong," he said. "The trends over the next few quarters, I think, should be supportive." Risks could arise after that, but it is "too early to call." 'Start of the end'Some analysts remain skeptical that Coreweave will be able to calm credit fears.Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, points out that the company is facing a huge bill in just over two years. CoreWeave owes roughly $15 billion in principal payments through 2028, according to its second-quarter earnings statement. "They don't have enough cash to service all that debt," he said. "Unless some big orders come in, unless some big money flows come in for them in the next 17, 18 months, I think this is going to be the start of the end for CoreWeave, unless somebody comes in and wants to buy them. But who wants to buy all that debt?" However, there could be a "small" window for the company to push out its debt for another three to five years, but it will depend on how strong their cash flow is when they report on Tuesday, Lang said. Plus, issuing equity to help fund infrastructure projects, like Meta and Oracle did recently, isn't an option for CoreWeave, he noted."They're going to dilute the stock so much that it's going to continue to go down," he said. "They missed that window when the stock was in the hundreds."CoreWeave topped $183 in June 2025. It has since declined more than 73%, recently trading around $47. Despite the fall, analysts remain bullish on the stock with an average overweight rating and $126 target, based on 39 estimates complied by FactSet.—CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed reporting.

schema.headline: CoreWeave earnings put debt-fueled AI build-out under scrutiny

title: Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling
description: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gestures as he speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. U.S.Ch
body: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gestures as he speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. U.S.Chip Somodevilla | Getty ImagesSecretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Tuesday railed against the Republican congressman who introduced articles of impeachment against him and aggressively defended his leadership in the Iran war and other military operations."What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said a day after Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., put forward the eight impeachment articles. "It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," Hegseth said during his first Pentagon news conference in six months.The articles accuse Hegseth of waging war in contravention of Congress, carrying out extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean against purported drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a military veteran.Massie, a libertarian who lost his Republican primary in May after clashing with President Donald Trump, kicked off the impeachment battle less than a week after a blue-wave midterm that will flip House and Senate control to Democrats.Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) discusses articles of impeachment he introduced against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the U.S. Capitol Building on November 09, 2026 in Washington, D.C.Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesRep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to be speaker of the House in the next Congress, on Sunday said Democrats are a "hard yes" on impeaching Hegseth. He reiterated his support on Monday in a press conference.The House is set to vote Tuesday on a procedural motion related to the impeachment resolution. If it passes, the measure will proceed to a debate and vote. Impeachment resolutions are privileged, meaning the House must act on them, table them or vote to refer them to committee within two legislative days.Hegseth accused Massie of performing a "stunt" that sends dangerous signals to America's enemies."It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time," Hegseth said. "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage."Trump piled on, writing in a Truth Social post right after Hegseth's presser ended that the Pentagon chief "gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!"Trump, who was impeached twice during his first presidential term, said Monday that he would stand by Hegseth even if the House impeaches him.Republicans hold a slim 218-214 majority in the House, but it is unclear if the rest of the GOP conference will be able to band together to defeat Massie's impeachment resolution. Some Republicans, notably including Vice President JD Vance, have directly blamed their midterm losses on the Iran war, which continues to see intermittent fighting amid an uneasy stalemate.If Hegseth is impeached, the Senate would be tasked with holding a trial and voting on whether to remove him from office. A two-thirds majority is required for conviction and removal. No U.S. Cabinet secretary has ever been removed by the Senate, though two have been impeached.— CNBC's Garrett Downs contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling

title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78, looks to start trading  Nov. 19, sources say
description: Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on
body: Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut. The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors.At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, rising from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May.Anthropic said it has entered into an agreement with Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to purchase $26 billion of the company's Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the IPO price. The shares sold in the private placement will not be registered in the offering and will not be subject to lock-up agreements with the underwriters, the company said.As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment, following last week's midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They're also facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases. CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch."Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under the ticker symbol "ANT," the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk's reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO. Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company's book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called frontier models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September. Anthropic said that the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month."Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it though."WATCH: Anthropic’s breakneck rise: What to know before the IPO

schema.headline: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78, looks to start trading  Nov. 19, sources say
